threads.thread_goal: Align on current customer journey and main pain points across channels.

messages.text:
Kicking off the customer journey mapping for our cross-channel customer experience upgrade project_title: Cross-Channel CX Upgrade.
For T1 we need a simple view of how customers move through store, contact centre, and field sales today, plus the main pain points.
Can each of you share, in one message, how a typical customer interaction starts and ends in your area, and the top 2–3 issues you see most often? We will later connect this to the shared feedback log in A5.
Once we have everyone’s input, we can agree on the high-level journey and pick 3–4 pain points to prioritise.

From the field sales side, a typical journey starts with either an inbound request from a store or an outbound visit we schedule.
Rough outline:
- Pre-visit: I review recent notes and any entries in A5 related to that store or account.
- Visit: greet, quick needs analysis, walk the floor, discuss promotions, agree next steps.
- Post-visit: send a short recap and confirm delivery or merchandising actions.
Top issues I see:
1) Misalignment between what we agree in the visit and what is actually implemented in-store.
2) Confusion on who owns follow-up when a customer complaint comes through the contact centre but relates to a store promotion.
3) Limited visibility of previous issues because notes are scattered, not always in A5.
For T1 I can sketch the field sales touchpoints in more detail if helpful.

Adding another sales account manager view.
Typical journey for me:
- Customer or store reaches out about a promotion or stock concern.
- I schedule a call or visit, do a basic needs discussion, then propose an offer.
- After that, I try to follow up by email or phone, but it is not always consistent.
Pain points I notice:
1) When a complaint comes from the store, I am not always sure if it was already logged in A5 or handled by the contact centre.
2) Different expectations on discounts or refunds depending on who the customer spoke to first.
3) It is hard to keep track of all follow-ups for T1 without a simple shared view.
Happy to adjust this once we see the full journey map.

From the specialised seller side in stores:
Journey usually looks like this:
- Customer walks in or calls the store directly.
- We greet, ask a couple of questions about what they are looking for, then walk them to the right area.
- We demonstrate products, explain services, and close the sale at the till.
- If there is an issue later, they either come back to the store or call the contact centre.
Main pain points:
1) Different answers on refunds and complaints depending on who they talk to first.
2) During busy times, we skip steps like checking if they found everything, which hurts experience.
3) We rarely log feedback in A5 unless it is a big issue, so smaller patterns are missed.
For T1 I can help list the in-store touchpoints in more detail, especially around advice and aftersales.

From food service in-store:
- Customer arrives, often in a hurry, and heads straight to the counter.
- We greet, take the order, sometimes suggest an extra item, then prepare and hand over.
- If they are not happy, they usually complain on the spot or later to the store manager.
Pain points I see:
1) At peak times we focus on speed and skip asking if everything was ok.
2) Cleanliness or display issues can affect how they feel before they even talk to us.
3) We do not have a simple habit of writing feedback into A5, so it stays verbal.
For T1 I can map the quick-service steps and where we could add one or two simple checks without slowing the line.

From the crop production worker side, I am less in front of customers but I do get some direct feedback when I help in the store or during deliveries.
What I see in the journey:
- Sometimes customers ask about product origin or quality when I am around.
- If there is a quality issue, they complain to the store first, and only later it reaches me.
Pain points:
1) Quality complaints are not always logged in A5, so we may repeat the same mistake.
2) It is not clear when I should be informed versus when the store just handles it.
For T1 I can help describe the handover points between store and supply side, especially for quality issues.

From the contact centre side, a typical journey:
- Customer calls or emails with a question, complaint, or order.
- We greet, identify the need, check basic info, and either resolve or escalate.
- If it is store-related, we call the store or send a message; if it is account-related, we pass it to a sales account manager.
Pain points we see:
1) Escalations are not always closed in a visible way, so the customer may call back.
2) Different handling of refunds and complaints between us and stores.
3) We do not always capture enough detail in A5, especially channel and follow-up owner.
I will start drafting the journey map for T1 based on all your inputs and share a simple diagram later today.

Thanks for pulling this together.
To help you with T1, I suggest we structure the journey in three big stages across all channels:
1) Discover and decide: first contact, questions, advice.
2) Buy and receive: transaction, delivery or immediate use.
3) Use and resolve: aftersales, complaints, repeat purchase.
Each of us can then plug our touchpoints into those stages. That should make it easier to align later with the playbook and A5 fields.

I like those three stages.
If we go with that, in-store touchpoints would be:
- Discover and decide: greeting, needs questions, product demo.
- Buy and receive: checkout, packaging, quick reminder of key info.
- Use and resolve: returns desk, complaint handling, small fixes.
This lines up well with what we will later define in the refunds and complaints policy and the job aids, and it should be easy to reflect in A5 as well.

Agree on the three stages.
For food service, the main pain points across those stages are:
- Discover and decide: customers not seeing clear menus or offers.
- Buy and receive: long waits and rushed handover.
- Use and resolve: complaints about temperature or freshness not always logged.
These feel like they should be in the top list we focus on in the playbook.

From my side, mapping to those stages:
- Discover and decide: questions about product origin or quality.
- Buy and receive: issues with packaging or freshness at handover.
- Use and resolve: quality complaints that should be logged in A5 but sometimes are not.
This reinforces that inconsistent logging and follow-up is a big pain point.

Using those three stages, the main issues I see from my accounts are:
- Discover and decide: customers get different advice depending on who they talk to.
- Buy and receive: confusion on promotions and conditions agreed in the field versus in-store.
- Use and resolve: unclear ownership for follow-up when a complaint starts in the contact centre.
These might be candidates for our top pain points list.

I have drafted a simple journey map for T1 using the three stages suggested and added the main touchpoints for each role.
Before we lock it in, can you all confirm that this structure works for you:
1) Discover and decide.
2) Buy and receive.
3) Use and resolve.
If yes, we can treat this as our shared journey for the project and move on to selecting the top 3–4 pain points to prioritise in the playbook.

Confirmed from my side. Those three stages cover all field sales interactions and will be easy to explain to stakeholders.
I suggest we also note in A5 which stage the feedback relates to, but we can keep that as a simple optional field to avoid complexity.

Works for me too. It matches how we talk to customers in-store and how we handle aftersales.
On pain points, based on what everyone shared, I see these as common across channels:
1) Inconsistent handling of refunds and complaints.
2) Weak or missing logging of feedback in A5.
3) Misalignment between what is promised in one channel and delivered in another.
We might add a fourth around rushed interactions at peak times.

Agree with that list.
From the counter, the rushed interactions at peak times are very visible, and they connect to the other issues because we skip steps like explaining refund options or capturing feedback.
So I would support those four as our focus.

I am aligned as well.
The inconsistent logging in A5 and unclear ownership of follow-up are the ones that affect my work most, but they are linked to the same four points you listed.

From my accounts, those four pain points also show up.
Especially misalignment between what is promised in the field and what happens in-store, and different answers on refunds.
I am ok to use these as the main focus for the playbook.

Thanks all, summarising so we can close this thread for T1.
Shared journey: three stages across all channels – discover and decide, buy and receive, use and resolve. We will use this as the base map for the project.
Top four pain points to prioritise in the playbook:
1) Inconsistent handling of refunds and complaints.
2) Weak or missing logging of feedback in A5.
3) Misalignment between what is promised in one channel and delivered in another.
4) Rushed interactions at peak times leading to skipped key steps.
Unless anyone objects today, we will treat this as agreed and move on to the playbook outline.

threads.thread_goal: Define the structure and core behaviours of the unified playbook.

messages.text:
As a follow-up to the journey mapping, I have drafted an outline for the unified customer experience playbook in A1, linked to T2.
Structure so far:
1) Introduction and principles.
2) Common behaviours across all channels.
3) Store experience.
4) Contact centre experience.
5) Field sales and account management.
6) Customer feedback and reporting using A5.
Can you review this structure and suggest changes before we lock it in? We also need to agree on 3–5 core behaviours that should be common across all channels.

Thanks for sharing the outline.
From a field sales perspective, I like that there is a dedicated section plus a common behaviours section.
For T5, I suggest we align the field visit script in A4 with the same three journey stages we agreed in T1, and then mirror that in A1.
On core behaviours, my first draft list would be:
- Consistent greeting and introduction.
- Simple needs analysis.
- Clear explanation of next steps and who owns follow-up.
- Logging key feedback in A5 when something goes wrong.
We can refine the wording together.

Looking at A1, the structure makes sense to me.
One question: in the field sales section for T5, can we include a short example of a visit recap email or call script? That would help me be more consistent.
On common behaviours, I would add something about using the same simple language on refunds and complaints, so customers do not hear different explanations depending on the channel.

I went through A1 and the outline looks workable for stores.
For the store section, I would suggest sub-sections:
- Greeting and first questions.
- Product advice and demonstrations.
- Checkout and closing.
- Handling refunds and complaints, aligned with A6.
On core behaviours across channels, I support what was proposed and would add one more: closing each interaction by checking if the customer has any other question.
That would give us four or five behaviours total.

From food service, the outline in A1 works as long as the store section leaves room for quick-service specifics.
For the common behaviours, I would phrase them in a way that fits short interactions, for example:
- Quick, friendly greeting.
- One simple question to understand the need.
- Short explanation of what will happen next.
- If there is an issue, say what we will do and, when needed, log it in A5.
That keeps it realistic for peak times.

I had a look at A1 as well.
For my role, the main part is the feedback and reporting section linked to A5.
Could we make sure that section includes a very simple example of how to fill in the sheet for a quality complaint, so that even people who do not usually talk to customers can use it when needed?
On core behaviours, I agree with the list so far and would not add more, to keep it simple.

Thanks for the feedback, I have updated A1 accordingly for T2:
- Added sub-sections in the store part as suggested.
- Linked the refunds and complaints part to A6.
- Added a simple example of a visit recap for T5.
- Expanded the feedback section with a filled-in example of A5.
On core behaviours, combining your inputs, the candidate list is now:
1) Consistent, friendly greeting.
2) Simple needs question.
3) Clear explanation of next steps and who will follow up.
4) Consistent explanation of refunds and complaints.
5) Logging key feedback in A5 when something goes wrong.
Can you confirm if we keep all five, or if we should reduce to four?

I would keep all five.
They are still easy to remember and they directly address the pain points we prioritised in T1.
From a field sales angle, they also map well to the visit script we will detail in A4 for T5.

Agree, five is fine.
In stores we can easily put these on a small card or poster later, and they cover both sales and problem situations.
No need to cut one out from my side.

I am ok with five as well.
For quick-service, we can group them into three short lines on the job aids later, but having the full five in A1 is useful for training.

From my side, five is still manageable.
The last one about logging in A5 is especially important for people like me who are not always in front of customers but sometimes receive complaints.

I am also fine with the five behaviours.
They will help me be more structured in calls and visits, especially around explaining next steps and logging issues.
No changes from my side.

Great, summarising the decisions for T2 so we can move forward.
1) We confirm the playbook structure in A1 with sections: introduction and principles, common behaviours, store, contact centre, field sales and account management, and customer feedback and reporting.
2) We adopt the five core behaviours across all channels:
- Consistent, friendly greeting.
- Simple needs question.
- Clear explanation of next steps and follow-up owner.
- Consistent explanation of refunds and complaints.
- Logging key feedback in A5 when something goes wrong.
I will mark this version of A1 as the approved outline and then we can deepen the channel-specific sections, including T4 and T5 content.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on in-store checklist, refunds policy, and job aids content.

messages.text:
I have put together a first draft of the in-store merchandising and cleanliness checklist in A2 for T3, based on our daily routines.
It is structured to be completed in under 5 minutes and covers:
- Entrance and first impression.
- Product displays and stock levels.
- Food service counter and seating area.
- Cleanliness of key zones.
I would like feedback from store and field colleagues, especially on anything missing or too detailed. This checklist will also feed into the job aids in A7 for T8.
Separately, we need to make sure it lines up with the refunds and complaints policy in A6 for T6, so that what we promise to customers matches what they see in-store.

Thanks for drafting A2.
From a specialised seller view, the structure works well. A few suggestions for T3:
- In the entrance section, add a quick check that key promotions are visible and not blocked.
- In the product displays part, include a line about price labels being clear and matching the till.
- For cleanliness, maybe group tasks by zone so staff can walk the store once instead of jumping around.
On A6 for T6, I have started drafting common rules for refunds and complaints. I will share wording shortly so we can check that the checklist and job aids in A7 reinforce the same expectations.

I reviewed A2 with a crop production lens.
For T3, could we add a simple check that fresh products are rotated correctly and that any items not meeting quality standards are removed from display?
This would help reduce quality complaints later and keep what customers see aligned with what we promise in A6.

From field sales, A2 looks practical.
For T3, I would only suggest adding a quick line about checking that any field-agreed displays or secondary placements are actually in place.
That way, when we visit, we are not surprised by missing displays that were part of a promotion.
On A6 for T6, I am keen that the policy clearly states what stores can decide on the spot versus what needs escalation, so we can reflect that in our visit script and in A7 job aids.

I had a quick look at A2 as well.
It seems clear, but I am not sure if some colleagues will find it too long.
Maybe we can bold or highlight the absolute must-do checks for T3, so that in very busy times they at least cover those.
On A6, I would appreciate a simple table of examples, like when a refund is ok immediately and when it needs approval, so I can explain it consistently to my accounts.

From the contact centre side, A2 looks good and will help us set expectations with customers.
For A6 and T6, I have added a draft section that explains how contact centre decisions on refunds and complaints should match what stores do, including when we can authorise something on the call and when we must refer to the store.
Once we agree the final wording, I will also update A3 so that the call flow reflects the same rules.

Here is the proposed structure for A6 under T6:
- Part 1: Principles (fairness, clarity, speed).
- Part 2: What stores can decide immediately (with examples).
- Part 3: What the contact centre can decide immediately.
- Part 4: When to escalate to a manager or account manager.
- Part 5: How to log the case in A5.
Example rules:
- If the product is clearly faulty and within a set time, store or contact centre can refund or replace.
- If the issue is about a promotion misunderstanding, we follow a simple rule: honour the lower price once, then correct the display.
Please review and suggest changes before we finalise the wording.

The structure for A6 makes sense to me.
For food service, I would add an example about complaints on temperature or freshness: if the customer raises it during the visit, we replace the item immediately and log it in A5; if it comes later, we follow the same faulty product rule.
On A2 for T3, I will incorporate the suggestions on promotions, price labels, and quality rotation, and I will mark the must-do checks for peak times.

I support the A6 structure.
For T6, could we also include a short note that if the same quality complaint appears several times in A5, it should be escalated to the supply side so we can check the source?
That would help us act on patterns, not just single cases.

From field sales, I like the clear split of decisions in A6.
For T6, I would just clarify in the escalation part when an account manager should be involved, for example:
- Repeated complaints from the same business customer.
- Disputes about contract terms or large orders.
That way we can also reflect it in the visit script in A4 and in the job aids in A7.

I agree with the structure and the examples in A6.
For me, the examples table will be very helpful when explaining to customers what we can do on the spot.
No extra changes from my side on T6.

From the contact centre view, I have added a couple of call examples into A6 and aligned the escalation rules with A3.
This should make it easier for agents to follow the same decisions as stores.
If there are no objections, I suggest we treat the current wording in A6 as final for T6 and move to sign-off on A2 and the core content for A7 job aids.

No objections from me.
The current A6 wording is clear and matches what we can realistically do in stores.
For A7 and T8, I propose that the job aids for frontline staff include:
- The five core behaviours from A1.
- A very short summary of the refunds and complaints rules from A6.
- A reminder to log key issues in A5.
That should keep them short enough to post in back-of-house areas.

I have now updated A2 for T3 with all the suggestions and tested it in a quick run-through. It can still be done in under 5 minutes.
I also drafted a first version of A7 for T8 with the elements you listed: core behaviours, short refunds and complaints summary, and A5 reminder.
Unless anyone spots a major gap, I think we are ready to sign off A2 and confirm the A6 wording.

I checked the latest A2 and it looks good to me.
The quality rotation and removal of non-compliant items are clearly included.
No further comments.

Same here, A2 and A6 both look aligned with what we discuss in the field.
The job aid content in A7 will also help when we do store walks with managers.
Happy to proceed.

I am ok with A2 and A6 as they are now.
The examples in A6 will be especially useful for me.
No extra changes.

To close this thread:
- We confirm A2 as the final version of the merchandising and cleanliness checklist for T3.
- We approve the current wording of A6 as the cross-channel refunds and complaints policy for T6.
- We agree on the core content for A7 job aids under T8: five core behaviours, short refunds and complaints summary, and A5 logging reminder.
I will update our overall playbook draft in A1 to reference A2, A6, and A7 accordingly.

threads.thread_goal: Plan pilot, training sessions, and feedback collection approach.

messages.text:
Now that we have the main playbook pieces in place in A1, A2, A3, A4, A6, and A7, we need to plan the pilot and training.
Proposal for pilot scope under T11 and T12:
- One medium-traffic store with food service.
- One smaller store without food service.
- One key account for field sales.
For training under T9, I suggest short sessions per role (max 2 hours total per person) focusing on the five core behaviours and how to use A5 and A8.
For reporting under T7 and T10, we would use A5 for daily feedback and A8 for weekly metrics.
Please share your thoughts on which locations and participants make sense, and any constraints on training times.

For the field sales part of the pilot under T11, I suggest we pick the key account where we already have regular visits and a cooperative store manager.
That will make it easier to test the visit script in A4 and the cross-channel refunds policy in A6.
On training for T9, I can run a short session with the account team to walk through A4, A5, and A8, focusing on how to capture commitments and feedback consistently.

I am happy to join the pilot on the account side, but I would prefer if we keep the training session very practical.
Maybe we can do one short group call where we walk through a sample visit using A4 and then a quick exercise on filling A5 and A8.
I will need help setting up the weekly reporting routine for T10, as I am not used to tracking metrics regularly.

For stores, I recommend we choose:
- One medium-traffic store with food service where we know the team is open to trying new routines.
- One smaller store without food service but with a strong store manager.
This will let us test A2 and A7 in two different environments under T11.
For training under T9, we can do two short huddles per store: one focused on the five core behaviours and A7, and one on A2, A6, and A5.
We just need to schedule them around shift changes to stay within the 2-hour limit.

I agree with the store choices suggested.
For food service, I can support the medium-traffic store pilot under T11 and help run the huddles for T9.
We can use A7 job aids as the main visual, and do a quick walk-through of A2 and how it links to customer experience.
On timing, early morning before opening or just after shift change tends to work best.

From my side, I can join the pilot by helping the medium-traffic store log quality-related feedback in A5 under T7.
I can also support a short explanation during one of the huddles on what kind of issues should be escalated to the supply side.
For T10, I can help check that the weekly A8 report reflects any repeated quality issues.

Thanks for the inputs.
On the contact centre side for T9 and T11:
- We will run one 60-minute virtual session to cover A3, A6, and A5, focusing on the new call flow and escalation rules.
- We will then do a 30-minute follow-up after the first pilot week to review A5 entries and A8 metrics.
For pilot locations, I will check with operations leadership to confirm the two stores and the key account you suggested. I will come back with names and dates so we can lock them in.

On metrics for T10 and A8, I propose we track at least these four during the pilot:
1) Number of complaints per week by channel.
2) Number of compliments or positive mentions.
3) Percentage of cases logged in A5 that were closed within an agreed time.
4) Number of times the refunds and complaints policy in A6 had to be escalated.
We can keep the format in A8 very simple: one line per week per location.

Those four metrics in A8 sound reasonable.
I might need a short guide or example on how to fill in the weekly report for T10, especially for the account side.
Maybe we can include one sample line in A8 for the key account pilot.

I like the metric set.
For stores, we can assign responsibility for updating A8 as follows under T10:
- Store manager: overall weekly numbers.
- One frontline champion per store: making sure A5 is filled in daily.
This should keep it manageable and clear.

I can act as the frontline champion for the medium-traffic store during the pilot under T11.
I will help the team remember to log issues in A5 and support the store manager with the A8 weekly update.
For T9, I will also prepare a very short handout summarising the training points for those who cannot attend live.

On the smaller store, I can support the frontline champion by checking A5 entries once a week and flagging any repeated quality issues.
This will help us use the pilot to improve not just service but also product quality.
No extra metrics needed from my side.

Quick update: I have checked with operations leadership and they are comfortable with the pilot scope we proposed.
Pilot locations under T11:
- Store A: medium-traffic with food service.
- Store B: smaller format without food service.
- Key Account X: managed by the field sales team.
We will run the pilot for two weeks, using A5 daily and A8 weekly.
Next step is to lock the training schedule for T9 and confirm who attends which session.

For T9, on the field side I propose:
- One 60-minute virtual session for all account managers involved in Key Account X.
- A 30-minute follow-up after week one of the pilot to review A5 and A8 entries.
I can host both sessions and will coordinate with you on timing.

That works for me.
If we can schedule the main session early next week and the follow-up at the end of the first pilot week, that would be ideal.
I will make sure to attend both and bring any questions from the account side.

For stores under T9, I suggest:
- Store A: two 30-minute huddles in the same week, one focused on A7 and core behaviours, one on A2, A6, and A5.
- Store B: same structure, adjusted to their staffing.
We can run these at shift change times to minimise disruption.
I can coordinate with store managers to finalise exact slots.

I am aligned with that plan.
I will support the Store A huddles and help prepare a simple attendance sheet so we can track who has received which part of the training for T9.
We can then share attendance summaries as part of the weekly A8 report.

For Store B, I can help the manager with the attendance tracking and make sure the team understands how to fill in A5.
This should keep the reporting routine under T7 and T10 simple enough for everyone.

Summarising the plan so we can close this thread:
Pilot scope under T11:
- Store A (medium-traffic with food service).
- Store B (smaller format).
- Key Account X for field sales.
Training schedule under T9:
- Contact centre: 60-minute session plus 30-minute follow-up.
- Field sales: 60-minute session plus 30-minute follow-up.
- Stores: two 30-minute huddles per store in the same week.
Reporting routine under T7 and T10:
- A5 used daily in all pilot locations to log issues and feedback.
- A8 updated weekly with the four agreed indicators and training attendance summary.
If there are no objections by tomorrow, we will treat this as agreed and move on to executing T11 and then updating A1 for final sign-off in T12.
